QuadraticMap.toContinuousMultilinearMap.text: The formal definition takes the full polar form of a real quadratic form $Q$ and includes its continuity in finite dimensions. Its value remains $Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$. In particular, the diagonal is $2Q(h)$; continuity does not change that factor or turn this construction into the half polar form.

QuadraticMap.toContinuousMultilinearMapH.text: The formal definition uses the continuous half polar form of $Q$ on a finite-dimensional real normed space. Its value at $(u,v)$ is $\tfrac12[Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)]$. At $(h,h)$ this is $Q(h)$, which is the normalization needed to transfer positive definiteness of $Q$ to the lower-bound argument.

QuadraticMap.toContinuousMultilinearMap_.text: The formal statement identifies the value of the continuous full polar form with $Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$. It assumes a finite-dimensional real normed space and an arbitrary quadratic form $Q$. This confirms that adding continuity to the construction leaves its values unchanged; no factor of one half is present.

The formal statement identifies the value of the continuous half polar form with $\tfrac12[Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)]$. It assumes a finite-dimensional real normed space and an arbitrary quadratic form $Q$. For the Hessian quadratic form, the displayed polar identity therefore gives $\tfrac12[B(u,v)+B(v,u)]$ at every pair of vectors.

QuadraticMap.toMultilinearMap.text: For a real quadratic form $Q$, the formal definition uses the full polar form $P(u,v)=Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$. It is linear in each argument. On the diagonal, $P(h,h)=2Q(h)$, so this definition must be distinguished from the half polar form that recovers $Q$ on the diagonal.

QuadraticMap.toMultilinearMapHalfPolarBi.text: The formal definition takes $\tfrac12[Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)]$ for a real quadratic form $Q$. This is the half polar form. Its diagonal value is $Q(h)$, unlike the full polar form whose diagonal is $2Q(h)$. No finite-dimensional assumption or positivity assumption is needed for this algebraic construction.

On a finite-dimensional real normed space, the half polar form $\tfrac12[Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)]$ is continuous in both arguments jointly. This statement applies to every quadratic form $Q$, without a positivity assumption. Continuity is used later when the form is restricted to the compact unit sphere.

QuadraticMap.toMultilinearMap_continuous.text: On a finite-dimensional real normed space, the full polar form $P(u,v)=Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$ of every quadratic form $Q$ is continuous in the pair of arguments. The statement uses finite dimensionality to obtain continuity. It does not require $Q$ to be positive definite or to arise from a Hessian.

coercive_of_posdef.text: On a finite-dimensional real normed space, positivity of $D^2f(a)[h,h]$ for every nonzero $h$ gives some $C>0$ with $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$ for all $h$. The formal statement requires neither analyticity, a zero gradient nor a separate smoothness assumption. Its conclusion is a bound on the Hessian, not yet a minimum of $f$.

coercive_of_posdefHalf.text: For a positive definite quadratic form $Q$ on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the formal statement gives a constant $C>0$ such that its half polar form at $(h,h)$ is at least $C\lVert h\rVert^2$ for every $h$. Since that diagonal value is $Q(h)$, this is the required quadratic lower bound.

coercive_of_posdef_of_contdiff.text: For a real-valued function on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the formal statement assumes smoothness of all orders at $a$ and positivity of $D^2f(a)[h,h]$ for nonzero $h$. It gives some $C>0$ with $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$ for every $h$. The proof uses smoothness to obtain Hessian symmetry.

continuousBilinearMapOfContinuousMultili.text: The formal definition evaluates a continuous map that is linear in each of two vector arguments as a bilinear form, with the value at $(u,v)$ unchanged. Its setting is a finite-dimensional normed space over a complete nontrivially normed field, including the real spaces used here. It makes no positivity or symmetry assertion.

coupled_spring_potential.text: There is a neighbourhood of the origin on which $U(0)\le U(x)$. The formal statement gives this non-strict local inequality. It does not state strictness away from the origin, uniqueness or a global inequality. The page presents those further conclusions separately through the completed-square argument and supplementary proofs.

couplingPotential.text: The formal definition assigns $U(x)=x_0^2+x_0x_1+x_1^2$ to every point of the real plane. It contains no spring constant, mass or equation of motion. Those quantities belong to the mechanical interpretation later in the page, where the physical potential energy is $kU(x)$.

couplingPotential_analyticAt.text: The potential $U$ is analytic at every point of the real plane. The source obtains this from the coordinate functions by taking squares, a product and sums, matching the polynomial formula. No restriction to the origin and no hypothesis about a displacement being small appear in the formal statement.

couplingPotential_gradient_zero.text: The formal statement is $\nabla U(0)=0$. Its proof uses the derivative formula and the correspondence between a derivative and a gradient in the Euclidean plane. This establishes the critical-point hypothesis for the minimum test; it does not by itself classify the critical point as a minimum.

couplingPotential_hasFDerivAt.text: At an arbitrary point $x$, the derivative sends an increment $h$ to $(2x_0+x_1)h_0+(x_0+2x_1)h_1$. The formal statement identifies this linear functional as the derivative of $U$. It is the derivative on the whole real plane; the vanishing of its coefficients at the origin is established separately.

couplingPotential_iteratedFDeriv_two.text: For every base point $z$ and vectors $u,v$, the formal statement gives $D^2U(z)[u,v]=2u_0v_0+u_0v_1+u_1v_0+2u_1v_1$. These four coefficients are the entries of $K$. The formula is independent of $z$ and allows distinct vectors in the two positions, so it specifies the full Hessian rather than only its diagonal values.

couplingPotential_posDef.text: The formal statement gives $D^2U(0)[h,h]>0$ for every nonzero vector $h$. The proof substitutes the explicit Hessian formula and uses nonnegativity of squares. It supplies the positivity hypothesis for the analytic test. The numerical estimate $D^2U(0)[h,h]\ge\lVert h\rVert^2$ appears in the page but is not the conclusion of this theorem.

hessianBilinearCompanion.text: Writing $B(u,v)=D^2f(a)[u,v]$, the formal definition forms the bilinear map $B(u,v)+B(v,u)$. This is a sum, not an average. When the Hessian is symmetric it equals $2B(u,v)$. It serves as the polar form of $Q(h)=B(h,h)$ and explains the factor of one half used later.

isLocalMin.of_subsingleton.text: If a topological space has at most one point, every real-valued function has a local minimum at each point of that space. No differentiability or vector-space hypothesis is needed. The zero-dimensional vector space in the page is an instance of this statement, allowing the analytic test to handle that case separately.

isLocalMin_of_posDef_of_littleo.text: The formal statement assumes a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a quadratic Taylor remainder $o(\lVert x-a\rVert^2)$, zero gradient, smoothness of all orders at $a$, and a positive definite Hessian there. It concludes a local minimum. The proof obtains the lower bound twice and uses smoothness in the second call; the page argues that this second call can be omitted.

iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap.text: The formal definition is $Q(h)=D^2f(a)[h,h]$. It establishes the quadratic dependence on $h$ and the identity relating $Q(u+v)$ to $Q(u)$, $Q(v)$ and the associated polar form. This construction alone assumes neither analyticity nor positive definiteness; those are separate hypotheses in the subsequent minimum test.

iteratedFDeriv_two_swap.text: The formal statement assumes that $f$ is smooth of all orders at $a$ in a real normed space. It concludes $D^2f(a)[u,v]=D^2f(a)[v,u]$ for every pair of vectors. This symmetry is the step used to identify half the polar form with the Hessian in the lower-bound proof that assumes smoothness.

le_of_littleO.text: Fix $x$ and write $h=x-a$. The formal statement assumes $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$, $Df(a)[h]=0$, and $|f(x)-f(a)-Df(a)[h]-\tfrac12D^2f(a)[h,h]|\le\tfrac C2\lVert h\rVert^2$. It concludes $f(a)\le f(x)$. This is a pointwise implication; it neither chooses a neighbourhood nor assumes a little-o estimate itself. No finite-dimensional assumption is imposed.

littleO_of_powerseries.text: If $f$ agrees with a convergent power series on a ball of positive radius around $a$, the formal statement gives a remainder $o(\lVert x-a\rVert^2)$ after subtracting the terms of degrees zero, one and two. It works on a real normed space without requiring finite dimensionality or a zero gradient; the linear term vanishes only at a critical point.

polarBilin_iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap.text: With $B(u,v)=D^2f(a)[u,v]$ and $Q(h)=B(h,h)$, the formal statement is $Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)=B(u,v)+B(v,u)$. No smoothness assumption is needed for this identity on a real normed space. It gives the sum of the two orders; identifying half that sum with $B$ off the diagonal additionally requires symmetry.

second_derivative_test.text: Let $f$ be real-valued on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The formal statement assumes a convergent power series on a ball of positive radius around $a$, zero gradient there, and a positive definite Hessian. It concludes a local minimum. Its proof obtains smoothness from the power series before applying the remainder argument.

second_derivative_test_analyticAt.text: Let $f$ be real-valued on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The formal statement assumes that $f$ is analytic at $a$, that $\nabla f(a)=0$, and that $D^2f(a)[h,h]>0$ whenever $h\ne0$. It concludes $f(a)\le f(x)$ throughout some neighbourhood of $a$. The conclusion does not include strictness or an explicit neighbourhood size.
